 How much Social Security increases each year you wait depends on your full retirement age, early-claiming cuts and 8% delayed credits, shown here age by age from 62 to 70
 1 / 12 List slides How a $2,000 Social Security benefit changes from age 62 to 70 List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated November 4, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 The same work record can produce two very different Social Security checks. A worker whose full retirement age is 67 and who claims at 62 receives 70% of the full benefit. If that worker waits until 70, the check rises to 124%. That makes the later check about 77% larger each month, and the cut for claiming early is permanent.
 The answer to how much Social Security increases each year you wait depends on which side of full retirement age a person is on. Before that age, every month of waiting shrinks a reduction the Social Security Administration applies for early claiming. After it, every month adds a delayed retirement credit worth 2/3 of 1%. That works out to 8% a year for anyone born in 1943 or later. The credits stop accruing at 70.
 Full retirement age is not the same for everyone. It is 66 for people born from 1943 to 1954 and 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later. For birth years 1955 through 1959, it rises two months per year. Claiming at 62 leaves 75% of the full benefit when full retirement age is 66, compared with 70% when it is 67. Waiting until 70 pays 132% in the first case and 124% in the second.
 The math does not end with the worker's own check. Delayed credits raise the benefit a surviving spouse can receive, but they do not raise a spousal benefit paid while both partners are alive. Working while claiming before full retirement age can trigger an earnings test that temporarily withholds payments. Cost-of-living adjustments, federal income taxes and the separate Medicare timeline at 65 also shape what a household receives.
 The 10 slides below lay out each rule in turn. They cover retirement ages by birth year, the formulas behind the cuts and credits, an age-by-age payment table and simple break-even calculations. They also cover the rules for spouses, survivors, working claimants, taxes and Medicare. No single claiming age fits every household. Health, work plans, marital status and other income all change how the trade-off between a smaller check sooner and a larger check later plays out.
 Full retirement age by birth year for Social Security 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Full retirement age is 66 for anyone born from 1943 through 1954 and 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later. For the birth years 1955 through 1959, it rises by two months for each year, under Social Security Administration rules.
 That middle group follows a fixed schedule. Someone born in 1955 reaches full retirement age at 66 and two months. A 1956 birth year moves it to 66 and four months. For 1957, it is 66 and six months. For 1958, it is 66 and eight months. People born in 1959 reach it at 66 and 10 months.
 The age matters because the Social Security Administration measures every claiming decision against it. The monthly amount paid at full retirement age is the full, unreduced benefit. Claiming before that age triggers a reduction. Waiting past it raises the check through delayed retirement credits.
 The two ends of the claiming range do not move. The earliest age to start retirement benefits is 62 for every birth year. Delayed credits stop building at 70 for every birth year. Only the midpoint shifts.
 That shifting midpoint changes the length of both windows. With a full retirement age of 67, the early window runs 60 months and the delay window runs 36 months. With a full retirement age of 66, each window runs 48 months. A longer early window means a deeper possible cut at 62. A shorter delay window means fewer months of credits before 70.
 The exact birth-year figure matters because the early reduction and the delayed credits are both calculated month by month. A person born in 1958 who assumes a full retirement age of 66 would misplace the starting point by eight months. Any estimate of a claim at 62 or at 70 would be off as a result.
 Full retirement age is a benefit-calculation term, not a required stopping point for work. Every figure tied to claiming early or late is calculated from this one age. That includes the size of the cut at 62 and the size of the raise at 70.
 How Social Security reduces benefits for claiming before full retirement age 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Claiming Social Security retirement benefits before full retirement age permanently shrinks every monthly check. The Social Security Administration calculates the cut month by month, and starting at 62 removes 30% of the full benefit for anyone whose full retirement age is 67.
 The formula has two tiers. Each of the 36 months closest to full retirement age lowers the benefit by 5/9 of 1%. That equals about 0.56% a month, or about 6.67% for each full year.
 Every month beyond those 36 is reduced at a smaller rate of 5/12 of 1%. That comes to 5% for each additional year. Only claimants who start more than three years before full retirement age reach the second tier.
 The two tiers add up at 62. Someone with a full retirement age of 67 who claims at 62 is 60 months early. The first 36 months subtract 20%. The remaining 24 months subtract another 10%, for the full 30% cut.
 A person whose full retirement age is 66 is 48 months early at 62. The first tier again takes 20%. The extra 12 months take 5%, for a total reduction of 25%.
 People born from 1955 to 1959 fall between those two cases. Their full retirement age sits between 66 and 67. Someone born in 1957 has a full retirement age of 66 and six months. Claiming at 62 puts that person 54 months early. The first 36 months cost 20%, and the next 18 cost 7.5%. The total cut is 27.5%, leaving 72.5% of the full benefit.
 Claiming closer to full retirement age shrinks the reduction. Starting 12 months early costs about 6.67% of the full benefit, all of it charged at the first-tier rate. Starting 24 months early costs about 13.33%. Starting 36 months early costs exactly 20%.
 The second tier is cheaper per month than the first. Each of the 36 months nearest full retirement age costs about 0.56%. Each earlier month costs about 0.42%. Both rates apply to the same base, the full benefit.
 The Social Security Administration treats the reduction as permanent. The smaller payment does not rise back to the full amount when the claimant later reaches full retirement age. An early claimant receives checks for more months, but each check stays smaller for life.
 Delayed retirement credits add 8% for each year past full retirement age 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Social Security pays delayed retirement credits worth 8% of the full benefit for every year a worker waits to claim beyond full retirement age. That rate applies to anyone born in 1943 or later.
 The Social Security Administration calculates the credit monthly, not annually. Each month of delay past full retirement age adds two-thirds of 1% to the benefit. A full year of those monthly increments produces the 8% annual figure.
 The credits begin only once a worker reaches full retirement age. Waiting from 62 up to full retirement age shrinks or removes the early-claiming reduction, but it does not earn delayed credits. The 8% rate applies strictly to the stretch between full retirement age and 70.
 Each year adds a fixed 8 percentage points of the full benefit. The increase does not compound on itself. Three years of delay add 24%, not a larger amount built on top of the previous year's raise.
 Birth year determines how many years of credits are available. A worker born in 1960 or later has a full retirement age of 67. That leaves three years to accumulate credits before 70, for a maximum of 124% of the full benefit.
 A worker born between 1943 and 1954 has a full retirement age of 66. That leaves four years of potential credits and a maximum of 132%. People born from 1955 through 1959 fall in between. Their full retirement age rises by two months per birth year. Each step removes two months of potential credits. Someone born in 1957, for example, reaches full retirement age at 66 and six months and can earn up to 28% in credits by 70.
 The credits attach to the worker's own retirement benefit. They change the size of the check paid on that person's earnings record. The 8% rate stays the same whatever the size of the underlying benefit. A larger full benefit therefore gains more dollars from each year of delay.
 What a $2,000 Social Security benefit pays at every age from 62 to 70 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A worker with a $2,000 full benefit and a full retirement age of 67 would collect $1,400 a month by claiming at 62 and $2,480 by claiming at 70. Each year of waiting in between raises the monthly check, but the size of the raise changes along the way.
 The $2,000 figure is a round number chosen for illustration. It is not an average or typical benefit. The percentages behind it come from Social Security Administration rules, so the same pattern holds at any benefit size. A worker with a $1,000 full benefit would see every dollar figure here cut in half.
 The earliest years climb in even steps. Waiting from 62 until 63 lifts the check to $1,500, or 75% of the full benefit. Waiting until 64 brings it to $1,600, or 80%. Each of those two years adds $100 a month.
 The pace picks up between 64 and full retirement age. At 65, the check is about $1,733. At 66, it is about $1,867. At 67, the worker receives the full $2,000. Each of those three years adds roughly $133 a month. The larger step reflects how the early-claiming reduction works. It takes a bigger cut per month in the three years closest to full retirement age than in the years further out.
 After 67, the steps grow again. Delayed retirement credits push the payment to $2,160 at 68, $2,320 at 69 and $2,480 at 70. Each year past full retirement age adds $160 a month, the largest annual step anywhere in the range.
 Grouping the years shows where most of the gain sits. The five years from 62 to 67 add $600 to the monthly check, an average of $120 for each year waited. The three years from 67 to 70 add another $480, or $160 for each year. Per year of waiting, the later stretch adds more money than the earlier one.
 Over a full year of checks, the age-70 claimant in this example collects $12,960 more than the age-62 claimant, before taxes.
 The comparison shifts slightly for workers whose full retirement age is 66. On the same $2,000 full benefit, they would receive $1,500 a month at 62 and $2,640 at 70. That age-62 check matches what a worker with a full retirement age of 67 gets by waiting until 63. For these earlier birth years, the age-70 check is about 76% larger than the age-62 check. The monthly gap widens to $1,140.
 These figures are fixed illustrations of monthly checks. They leave out annual inflation adjustments and income taxes, and they do not show lifetime totals. A larger check that starts later also arrives fewer times.
 Why Social Security delayed credits stop at age 70 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Social Security delayed retirement credits stop building at age 70, the point where a worker's own monthly retirement benefit reaches its maximum. Under Social Security Administration rules, waiting past 70 to file adds nothing more to the check.
 Credits start accruing in the month a worker reaches full retirement age and keep adding up until the month they turn 70. Those are the only months that count. A worker who files at 71 or 72 gets the same base benefit as someone with an identical earnings record who filed at 70. The extra years of waiting produce no larger payment.
 That makes 70 a firm boundary for anyone using delay to raise their payment.
 Credits are counted month by month, not in whole-year blocks. A worker does not need to wait a full year to see an increase. Someone with a full retirement age of 67 who files at 67 and six months earns six months of credits, a 4% increase. Filing at 68 and three months earns 15 months of credits, or 10%.
 Monthly accrual also means the filing date does not have to line up with a birthday. A worker can file in whichever month fits their job, health or household plans. The increase reflects exactly the number of months waited.
 The cap is fixed at 70, but full retirement age has moved. As a result, the largest possible gain from delay depends on birth year. A worker with a full retirement age of 66 can earn up to four years, or 48 months, of credits. That is a total increase of 32% over the full benefit.
 A full retirement age of 67 leaves three years, or 36 months, of credits before the cap. The maximum increase in that case is 24%. The later retirement age cuts the potential gain from waiting by eight percentage points.
 Workers born from 1955 to 1959 fall in between. Someone born in 1957, for example, has a full retirement age of 66 and six months. That leaves 42 months of credits before 70, worth a 28% increase.
 Break-even age for delaying Social Security from 62 or 67 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A simple break-even calculation puts the crossover near age 82.5 for someone who waits from a full retirement age of 67 until 70. For someone who waits from 62 to 67, it lands near age 78.7. Those ages mark when the larger, later checks catch up in total benefits collected.
 Break-even is a race between two payment streams. The person who claims earlier starts collecting sooner and builds a head start. The person who waits gets bigger checks but must make up for the months of payments never received. The break-even point is where the two running totals match.
 Both figures here assume a full retirement age of 67, which applies to anyone born in 1960 or later. The math runs on percentages of the full benefit. That means the results hold for a benefit of any size.
 Start with the wait from 67 to 70. Holding off means giving up 36 monthly checks at 100% of the full benefit. In return, each later check pays 124% instead of 100%, a gain of 24 percentage points a month. Dividing the 3,600 percent-months forgone by that 24-point gain gives 150 months, or 12.5 years. Counting from age 70, the crossover arrives near 82.5.
 The wait from 62 to 67 follows the same logic. Claiming at 62 would have paid 60 checks at 70% of the full benefit, a total of 4,200 percent-months. Waiting until 67 lifts each check by 30 points, from 70% to 100%. That gap closes after 140 months, about 11.7 years. Counting from age 67, the crossover lands near 78.7.
 Before each break-even age, the earlier claimant has collected more in total. After it, the person who waited pulls ahead, and the lead grows with every additional monthly payment.
 These are simple calculations, and they leave out several factors. They ignore cost-of-living adjustments, federal income taxes and investment returns. If early checks were saved and invested, the returns would push the crossover later. The math also looks at one worker's own benefit in isolation. It does not count anything a spouse or survivor might receive.
 Break-even does not predict how long any particular person will live, and it does not identify the right claiming age. A person's health, plans to keep earning a paycheck, whether a spouse relies on the work record and savings outside Social Security all bear on that choice. What the calculation does show is how long a delayed claim takes to pay off in total benefits — a reference point for weighing those personal factors.
 How delaying Social Security affects spousal benefits 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Waiting to claim does not make a spousal benefit any larger. Delayed retirement credits raise only the worker's own check, and the spousal benefit tops out at 50% of the worker's full benefit — the amount payable at the worker's full retirement age.
 The Social Security Administration sets the spousal maximum from that full benefit. It does not use the larger check a worker locks in by waiting past full retirement age. Credits earned between full retirement age and 70 stay with the worker.
 Take a worker with a $2,000 full benefit and a full retirement age of 67. The most a spouse can collect on that record is $1,000 a month. That ceiling holds whether the worker files at 67 or at 70.
 Household totals show the effect. With the worker claiming at 67 and the spouse at the maximum, the couple collects $3,000 a month. With the worker waiting until 70, the total is $3,480. The extra $480 is a 24% raise on the worker's check. On the couple's combined income, it is a 16% raise.
 Timing can also work against the spouse. A current spouse cannot collect a spousal benefit until the worker has filed for retirement benefits. A worker who waits until 70 can therefore also push back the start of the spouse's payments.
 The spouse's own claiming age decides how close the payment comes to the cap. The full 50% is available only when the spouse claims at or after the spouse's own full retirement age. A spouse who files earlier receives a permanently reduced amount.
 Waiting beyond that point adds nothing. Spousal benefits do not earn delayed retirement credits. A spouse who holds off past full retirement age gains nothing on the spousal portion.
 A spouse who also has a work record is paid that own benefit first. If the spousal amount is higher, the Social Security Administration adds the difference on top. The total equals the higher of the two amounts, not their sum.
 That leaves couples with two separate clocks. The worker's claiming age sets the size of the worker's check. The spouse's claiming age, measured against the spouse's own full retirement age, sets the size of the spousal check.
 How delaying Social Security raises survivor benefits 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A surviving spouse can receive up to the amount the deceased worker was getting, or was entitled to, at the time of death. That ceiling includes any delayed retirement credits the worker earned. A worker's claiming age therefore shapes two checks: the worker's own and the one a widow or widower may collect later.
 Social Security Administration rules count delayed credits toward the survivor benefit. The credits do not disappear when the worker dies. They become part of the amount the survivor's payment is measured against. This is the main reason waiting to claim can work as a form of protection for a spouse.
 The rule applies whether or not the worker had started collecting. A worker who died after passing full retirement age without filing had been building credits each month of the wait. Those credits are part of the benefit the worker was entitled to at death.
 The decision runs in both directions. A worker who claims before full retirement age accepts a permanent reduction. That smaller check also lowers the ceiling a survivor can reach. A worker who waits past full retirement age raises the ceiling with every month of delay, until the credits stop at 70.
 The survivor's own timing matters too. A widow or widower who starts survivor benefits before reaching full retirement age receives less than the full amount the worker's record supports.
 The effect is largest in a household where one spouse earned considerably more than the other. The higher earner's claiming age then sets the upper limit on the benefit available to whichever spouse outlives the other.
 The trade-off is not one-sided. Waiting means a couple gives up years of payments before the larger check begins. If the higher earner dies before 70, the survivor's ceiling reflects only the credits earned up to the date of death. The couple's health, savings, work plans and the age gap between the spouses all shape how that trade-off plays out.
 The Social Security earnings test for claiming early while working 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Claiming Social Security before full retirement age while still holding a job brings the earnings test into play. If pay from work goes above an annual limit, the Social Security Administration withholds some or all of the benefit for that year.
 The limit is not fixed. It changes every year. Any dollar figure tied to it belongs to a single calendar year. Anyone planning around it needs the threshold the agency publishes for that year, not a number remembered from an earlier one.
 Only earnings from work count toward the limit. Wages from a job and net earnings from self-employment are included. Pensions, investment income, interest and annuity payments are not.
 The test has a clear end point. It covers only the months before a person reaches full retirement age. Once that age arrives, earnings from a job no longer cause any withholding, however high the salary.
 Withholding is not a penalty. Money held back under the earnings test is not forfeited. When the worker reaches full retirement age, the agency recalculates the monthly benefit to give credit for the months in which checks were withheld. The result is a higher monthly payment from that point forward.
 That recalculation matters for anyone weighing an early claim. Each month a benefit starts ahead of full retirement age adds to a reduction that lasts for life. Crediting back the withheld months trims that reduction, because those months no longer count as months of early benefits.
 The timing still shapes household cash flow. A worker who claims at 62 and keeps earning above the limit may collect fewer checks in the first years than the benefit amount implies. The credit for those months comes later, built into a larger check after full retirement age, not as a lump-sum repayment.
 The earnings test never reaches a worker who waits. Someone who holds off until full retirement age, or later to collect delayed retirement credits, can keep working without any withholding. For people who expect a paycheck well into their 60s, that removes one variable from the claiming decision.
 Cost-of-living adjustments, taxes and Medicare when you delay Social Security 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Waiting to claim Social Security does not cost you any cost-of-living adjustments, which apply to your benefit whether or not you have started collecting. Federal taxes on benefits depend on income, and Medicare eligibility starts at 65 regardless of claiming age.
 A cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, is an annual percentage increase the Social Security Administration applies to benefits to reflect inflation. Delaying to 70 does not mean giving up years of those raises. The adjustments are built into a worker's benefit amount from age 62 onward, even before any check has been paid.
 That means delayed retirement credits stack on top of a benefit that has already absorbed every COLA announced during the waiting period. Each adjustment is a percentage. It therefore adds more dollars to a larger monthly payment than to a smaller one.
 Taxes run on a separate track. Whether benefits are taxed at the federal level depends on provisional income. The IRS calculates that figure by adding adjusted gross income, tax-exempt interest and half of a person's Social Security benefits. Depending on where that total falls, none of the benefit, part of it or up to 85% of it can count as taxable income. No more than 85% is ever taxed federally.
 Claiming age can change how that calculation plays out in a given year. A larger delayed check raises the half-of-benefits portion of provisional income. Someone who claims early while still drawing a salary may also see more of the benefit become taxable. The income thresholds that decide those shares are set in dollar terms. The IRS lists them in Publication 915, its guide to taxing Social Security benefits.
 Medicare follows its own clock. Eligibility generally starts at 65, regardless of whether a person has claimed retirement benefits. For anyone with a full retirement age of 66 or 67, Medicare coverage can begin before the full Social Security benefit is available.
 The two programs still connect at enrollment. People who already collect Social Security when they turn 65 are generally enrolled in Medicare Parts A and B automatically. People who are delaying their benefits are not. They need to sign up through the Social Security Administration. Missing the initial enrollment window can trigger a Part B late-enrollment penalty that lasts for as long as the person has that coverage.
